prohibited_recommendations: Do not discontinue immunosuppression abruptly — rejection risk.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy in GBS (they are part of baseline transplant regimen but not specifically for GBS).
required_recommendations: Coordinate with transplant team — adjust immunosuppression cautiously.
Initiate IVIG (preferred over plasma exchange in immunocompromised transplant recipient).
CMV PCR (serum and CSF) and EBV PCR given transplant status.
Pharmacology review for nephrotoxic and neurotoxic interactions.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP (post-lung transplant, likely immune dysregulation)

differential.key_features: Encephalopathy, tremor, and seizures more typical; chronic length-dependent neuropathy possible; trough levels and dose review.

differential.diagnosis: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease with CNS / nerve involvement
differential.key_features: EBV PCR, imaging, and CSF cytology; pattern typically focal rather than symmetric ascending.
Common opportunistic post-transplant; CSF CMV PCR and serum CMV PCR; usually marked CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis.
Post-transplant ICU course increases risk; symmetric ascending pattern less typical.

key_clinical_evidence: Solid-organ transplant recipients have multiple competing causes for new neuropathy — opportunistic infection, drug toxicity, PTLD — but GBS still occurs and remains diagnosable on the same Brighton criteria.
IVIG is generally preferred over PLEX in transplant recipients to avoid removing therapeutic immunosuppressant levels.
Coordinate medication review with transplant pharmacy — CNI and IVIG interaction, renal status.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Classic Brighton-level clinical pattern (areflexia, ascending weakness, CSF albuminocytologic dissociation, demyelinating EMG) defines GBS even in transplant recipients; opportunistic causes must be excluded but do not preclude the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Recent lung transplant with multiple immunosuppressants
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity or opportunistic infection rather than GBS.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: Two-week progressive lower extremity weakness with dizziness and difficulty walking, 4 months after bilateral lung transplant on triple immunosuppression.

past_medical_history: Bilateral lung transplant 4 months ago — indication: COPD end-stage

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F. is a 66-year-old bilateral lung transplant recipient presenting 4 months post-transplant with a 2-week history of progressive lower extremity weakness. He underwent uncomplicated bilateral lung transplantation 4 months ago for end-stage COPD. His immunosuppression regimen is tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone, with tacrolimus levels consistently therapeutic at 10.5 ng/mL on average over 3 months. He reports no recent infections, new medications, immunizations, or exposures. He denies respiratory illness or diarrheal illness. Two weeks ago he began noticing dizziness and generalized weakness with difficulty ambulating. The weakness has been specifically in his lower extremities and has progressed gradually — he initially needed a cane and now requires bilateral support. He has no upper extremity weakness and no sensory symptoms initially, though mild distal tingling developed in the second week. He initially had normal reflexes on exam, which became hypoactive and then absent at the ankles by week 3. The subacute 2-3 week progression on triple immunosuppression raised concern for a tacrolimus-related polyneuropathy (tacrolimus can cause demyelinating neuropathy), though levels are therapeutic. CMV and EBV (common post-transplant opportunistic infections) were tested and are negative.

neurological_exam.additional: Tacrolimus trough levels: target 8-12 ng/mL; average 10.5 ± 4.1 ng/mL over 3 months. No history of tacrolimus toxicity (no elevated levels). No recent infections, immunizations, or new medications. CMV PCR serum: negative. EBV PCR serum: negative. Brain MRI: normal. Insidious onset over 2 weeks, with total disease duration of approximately 4 weeks.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact upper extremities. Lower extremities limited by weakness.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Intact. No facial weakness. No ptosis.
neurological_exam.gait: Progressive inability to ambulate — requires bilateral support. Started with dizziness and difficulty 2 weeks ago; now cannot walk.
neurological_exam.motor: Lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3/5 bilaterally, knee extension 3/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5. Cannot walk without support. Upper extremity: normal (5/5).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Initially (week 1): deep tendon reflexes normal (2+) throughout. Week 3: hypoactive patellar (1+), absent Achilles bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: No sensory deficits at initial presentation. Mild distal tingling reported at 2-week follow-up.
